paragraphs.text: Many people still believe that the tongue is divided into separate zones for different tastes, with sweetness detected at the tip and bitterness at the back. This 'tongue map' appeared in textbooks for most of the twentieth century, but it is wrong. It originated in a 1901 study by the German scientist David Hänig, who found only slight differences in sensitivity across the tongue; a later translation exaggerated his findings. In fact, receptors for all basic tastes are found in taste buds across the whole tongue.

Scientists now generally recognise five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Umami, a savoury taste associated with foods such as meat, cheese and mushrooms, was first identified in 1908 by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda, who traced the distinctive flavour of a seaweed soup to a substance called glutamate. Western scientists remained sceptical for decades, and umami was widely accepted only after receptors for glutamate were discovered on the tongue in the early 2000s.

Each basic taste appears to have evolved for a reason. Sweetness signals energy-rich foods, saltiness helps maintain the body's balance of minerals, and umami indicates protein. Bitterness, by contrast, acts as a warning: many poisonous plants taste bitter, and humans have around 25 different bitter receptors, far more than for any other taste. Children are especially sensitive to bitter flavours, which may explain why many dislike vegetables such as broccoli.

What we call 'flavour', however, depends far more on smell than on taste. When we chew, aromas travel from the back of the mouth to the nose, and the brain combines these signals with information from the tongue. This is why food seems tasteless when we have a cold. Experts estimate that as much as 80% of flavour comes from smell. Sight and sound also play a role: in one experiment, people rated crisps as fresher and crunchier when the sound of their chewing was made louder through headphones.

Taste also changes with age. The number of taste buds declines after about the age of fifty, and the sense of smell weakens too, which can reduce appetite in elderly people and lead to poor nutrition. Some care homes now add stronger herbs and spices to meals to make food more appealing to residents.
